summary: The Hebrew imperative has three everyday forms — to a man, to a woman, to several people: לֵךְ! / לְכִי! / לְכוּ! “go!”, בּוֹא! / בּוֹאִי! / בּוֹאוּ! “come!”, חַכֵּה! / חַכִּי! / חַכּוּ! “wait!”. It is the future form without its prefix ת־: תֵּלֵךְ → לֵךְ, תָּבוֹא → בּוֹא, תִּסַּע → סַע, תְּחַכֶּה → חַכֵּה; nif‘al verbs put a הִ in front instead (תִּכָּנֵס → הִכָּנֵס “come in!”), hif‘il verbs change the vowel (תַּגִּיעַ → הַגַּע). In everyday speech many people simply use the future itself as the command — תָּבוֹא!, תְּחַכֶּה רֶגַע, תִּכָּנְסִי — which sounds more natural and often softer; the short imperative is a little more direct (and with some verbs formal). A prohibition is never made with the imperative: “don’t” is אַל + the future, אַל תֵּלֵךְ! “don’t go!”, אַל תְּחַכִּי “don’t wait (f.)”. Signs and general instructions use the infinitive: לֹא לְהִכָּנֵס “no entry”. Politeness comes from בְּבַקָּשָׁה “please”, not from a special verb form — there is no polite imperative. There is also a feminine plural imperative (לֵכְנָה), but it is literary; in speech the masculine plural is used for any group.

blocks.caption: The commands of the verbs you know. Several people: the future is תֵּלְכוּ, תָּבוֹאוּ … (“don’t” to several: אַל תֵּלְכוּ).
The imperative is the future without its prefix (nif‘al: הִ instead — תִּכָּנֵס → הִכָּנֵס).

blocks.title: Don’t = אַל + future
blocks.text: אַל תֵּלֵךְ! “don’t go!”, אַל תְּחַכִּי! “don’t wait! (f.)”, אַל תִּשָּׁאֲרוּ “don’t stay (pl.)”. Never *אַל לֵךְ and never *לֹא לֵךְ. (לֹא + future is a lasting rule: לֹא תִּגְנֹב “thou shalt not steal”.)

blocks.title: Speech prefers the future
blocks.text: Israelis often give a command with the plain future: תָּבוֹא מָחָר, תְּחַכֶּה רֶגַע, תִּכָּנְסִי. The short imperative (בּוֹא, חַכֵּה) is just as correct; it sounds more direct — and הִכָּנֵס, הַגַּע sound formal.

blocks.title: Three addressees
blocks.text: You must choose: to a man לֵךְ, to a woman לְכִי, to a group לְכוּ. The ending ־ִי is feminine, ־וּ plural — the same endings as in the future (תֵּלְכִי, תֵּלְכוּ).

blocks.title: Signs and instructions
blocks.text: A general instruction uses the infinitive: לֹא לְהִכָּנֵס “no entry”, נָא לְהַמְתִּין כָּאן “please wait here” (on a sign). Polite requests add בְּבַקָּשָׁה: הִכָּנֵס, בְּבַקָּשָׁה.

blocks.title: Ask yourself before you give an order
questions: Am I telling a man, a woman or several people?
Is it a prohibition? → אַל + future.
Do I want it direct (לֵךְ) or everyday-soft (תֵּלֵךְ)?
Is it a sign or a general rule? → the infinitive.

askYourself: Who is addressed: a man, a woman, several people?
Is it “do” or “don’t”? “Don’t” → אַל + the future (אַל תֵּלֵךְ / תֵּלְכִי / תֵּלְכוּ).
For “do”: take the future (תֵּלֵךְ) and drop the ת־ → לֵךְ; nif‘al: הִ + the rest (הִכָּנֵס).
Add the ending: ־ִי for a woman (לְכִי), ־וּ for several (לְכוּ).
Should it sound softer or more everyday? → use the future itself (תֵּלֵךְ, תָּבוֹאִי) and/or בְּבַקָּשָׁה.
Is it a sign, a recipe, a rule for everyone? → the infinitive (לֹא לְהִכָּנֵס).
steps: Positive: the imperative (or the future); negative: אַל + future.
Add the place, the object, and בְּבַקָּשָׁה if you want to be polite.

traps: *אַל לֵךְ → אַל תֵּלֵךְ (“don’t” always takes the future).
*בָּא! as a command → בּוֹא! (the imperative of בָּא has a holam).
לְכִי is to a woman, לְכוּ to several — do not use לֵךְ for everyone.
The feminine plural לֵכְנָה exists only in literary style; say לְכוּ to any group.

quiz.why: ־ִי is the ending for a woman; בּוֹא is to a man, בּוֹאוּ to several.
“Don’t” is אַל + the future, never with the imperative.

quiz.q: The imperative of תִּכָּנֵס (“you will come in”) is:
quiz.why: A nif‘al verb puts הִ where the future has ת: תִּכָּנֵס → הִכָּנֵס.

quiz.q: A sign at a door, “No entry”, says:
quiz.why: General instructions and signs use the infinitive: לֹא + לְהִכָּנֵס.

quiz.q: Which command sounds the most everyday, as Israelis say it?
quiz.why: In speech the future is the usual command; נָא is old-fashioned and the infinitive is for signs.

seeAlso.note: Arabic also builds the imperative from the prefix tense (تَذْهَبُ → اِذْهَبْ) and forbids with لَا + jussive (لَا تَذْهَبْ) — the same pattern as Hebrew אַל + future.
German geh! / geht! / gehen Sie! has a polite form and no gender; Hebrew has gender (לֵךְ / לְכִי) and no polite form — politeness is בְּבַקָּשָׁה.
Chinese verbs do not change: a command is the bare verb (来！), softened with 请 or 吧, and “don’t” is 别 / 不要 — like Hebrew אַל, a word of its own for prohibitions.

notes.text: Greek also has a singular and a plural imperative (πήγαινε / πηγαίνετε); Hebrew adds the feminine (לֵךְ / לְכִי / לְכוּ). Greek μην + subjunctive (μην πας) is close to אַל + future (אַל תֵּלֵךְ).
Like иди / идите, Hebrew has a singular and a plural — and a feminine too: לֵךְ / לְכִי / לְכוּ. There is no polite plural for one person; politeness is בְּבַקָּשָׁה.
Spanish says “don’t” with another form, not the imperative (no vayas); Hebrew does the same: אַל + future (אַל תֵּלֵךְ). There is no usted command (vaya).
English has one imperative for everyone (“Go!”); Hebrew chooses by the listener: לֵךְ (a man), לְכִי (a woman), לְכוּ (a group). “Don’t” is אַל + the future.
va / allez ~ לֵךְ / לְכוּ, plus a feminine, לְכִי; “ne va pas” is not built on the imperative in Hebrew: אַל תֵּלֵךְ.
German has one form per addressee too (geh! geht! gehen Sie!), but Hebrew has no polite Sie-form: politeness is בְּבַקָּשָׁה or the softer future.
Hindi grades the imperative by respect (जा / जाओ / जाइए); Hebrew grades it by gender and number (לֵךְ / לְכִי / לְכוּ), and “don’t” is אַל + future (मत जाओ ~ אַל תֵּלֵךְ).
Persian says “don’t” with a prefix on the imperative (نرو); Hebrew uses אַל + the future: אַל תֵּלֵךְ.
Arabic also has gendered imperatives (اِذْهَبْ / اِذْهَبِي / اِذْهَبُوا ~ לֵךְ / לְכִי / לְכוּ) and forbids with لَا + jussive (لَا تَذْهَبْ ~ אַל תֵּלֵךְ).
Turkish git! / gidin! has no gender; Hebrew adds a feminine (לֵךְ / לְכִי / לְכוּ). Turkish negates inside the verb (gitme!); Hebrew uses אַל + the future.
Japanese softens requests with verb forms (行ってください); Hebrew uses the future (תֵּלֵךְ) or בְּבַקָּשָׁה, and changes the form for a man, a woman or a group.
Korean imperatives change with the speech level (가 / 가세요 / 가십시오); Hebrew ones change with the listener’s gender and number.
Finnish has a singular and a plural imperative (mene! / menkää!) and a separate “don’t” form (älä mene!), as Hebrew has אַל תֵּלֵךְ; Hebrew adds a feminine: לְכִי.
Swahili has a singular and a plural imperative (nenda! / nendeni!); Hebrew adds a feminine: לֵךְ / לְכִי / לְכוּ.
Luganda uses the bare verb stem for one person (genda! “go!”) and another form for several; Hebrew has these two and a feminine as well.
Chinese has no imperative form (走!, 别走!); Hebrew changes the verb for the listener (לֵךְ / לְכִי / לְכוּ), and 别 ~ אַל + future: אַל תֵּלֵךְ.
Vietnamese uses the plain verb with particles (đi đi!, đừng đi!); Hebrew changes the verb for the listener, and đừng ~ אַל + future.
Inuktitut has imperative endings for one, two or several people; Hebrew has forms for a man, a woman and a group — no dual.
